title: Low-temperature oxide-ion conduction in Aurivillius-type ((Na0.5Bi0.5)n–1TinO3n)(Bi2O2) phases - Nature Energy
gist: A Chinese-led team reports Aurivillius-type ((Na0.5Bi0.5)n-1TinO3n)(Bi2O2) thin films (n = 4, 5, 7, 8) reaching oxide-ion conductivity of 0.025 S cm-1 at 350 °C, and builds fuel cells from a 4% Mg-doped (NBT)4/(BO)1 electrolyte that hit 0.726 W cm-2 at 400 °C. The record is a Nature Energy landing/abstract page, so only the abstract-level numbers, the mechanism attribution (bismuth-oxide intercalation creating dual-ion conduction pathways) and the author/funding block are available — no full experimental detail.

insights.claim: Aurivillius-type ((Na0.5Bi0.5)n-1TinO3n)(Bi2O2) thin films achieve oxide-ion conductivity of 0.025 S cm-1 at 350 °C, a regime where conventional solid oxide-ion conductors have too little ion mobility to be useful.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: 0.025 S cm-1 at 350 °C is the number to benchmark any low-temperature SOFC electrolyte claim against; if reproducible in bulk form it reopens intermediate-temperature fuel cell system designs that were shelved on materials grounds.
insights.quote: establish well-defined periodic fast ion-conducting channels allowing ionic conductivity of 0.025 S cm−1 at 350 °C
insights.locator: Abstract — 'These Aurivillius phases, characterized by periodic bismuth oxide layers'

insights.claim: Solid oxide-ion conductors today are confined to high-temperature (>500 °C) electrochemical energy technologies such as solid oxide fuel cells, and dropping that operating window would simplify system design, reduce degradation and broaden the usable material set.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Frames the entire commercial bottleneck for SOFCs — balance-of-plant cost and stack degradation are temperature-driven, so any electrolyte that works below 500 °C attacks both cost lines at once.
insights.quote: Operating these devices at lower temperatures could simplify system design, reduce degradation and broaden material options, but few conductors exhibit sufficient ion mobility in this regime.

insights.claim: The conductivity effect holds across a family rather than a single composition, with n = 4, 5, 7 and 8 members of the ((Na0.5Bi0.5)n-1TinO3n)(Bi2O2) series all reported as promising low-temperature conductors.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A tunable family rather than a one-off composition is what makes a materials result licensable — it gives a composition space to optimize and to patent around.
insights.locator: Abstract — 'Here we report a family of oxide-ion conductors'

themes.theme: Mechanism: bismuth-oxide intercalation and dual-ion pathways

insights.claim: The authors attribute the high low-temperature ionic conductivity of the Aurivillius films to localized lattice stretching plus dual-ion conduction pathways created specifically by intercalating bismuth oxide layers into a tetragonally distorted Na0.5Bi0.5TiO3 lattice.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: If layer intercalation — not doping — is the active lever, the same design rule can be transplanted to other layered oxides, which is where the follow-on IP will cluster.
insights.quote: we attribute these intriguing properties to localized lattice stretching and the unique dual-ion conduction pathways induced by the specific bismuth oxide intercalation

insights.claim: The mechanistic attribution rests on combining atomic-scale electron ptychography imaging with first-principles calculations, not on transport measurements alone.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
entities: Beijing National Center for Electron Microscopy
insights.so_what: Electron ptychography is becoming the standard evidentiary bar for atomic-scale energy-materials claims — a signal for demand in advanced electron microscopy instrumentation and for which labs can credibly publish here.
insights.locator: Abstract — 'Combining atomic-scale electron ptychography imaging with first-principles calculations'

insights.claim: Fuel cells built on the Aurivillius design reach a maximum power density of 0.726 W cm-2 at 400 °C, moving the result past a pure materials-characterization claim into demonstrated device output.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Device power density at 400 °C is the metric that decides whether a low-temperature SOFC can compete on stack size; 0.726 W cm-2 is the figure competitors and licensees will have to beat.
insights.quote: we constructed fuel cells that achieve a maximum power density of 0.726 W cm−2 at 400 °C, showing promising potential for technological applications

insights.claim: The electrolyte carried into the working fuel cell is a 4% Mg-doped (NBT)4/(BO)1 film, indicating the undoped parent film was not the composition used for the device demonstration.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The gap between the headline conductivity composition and the device composition is where scale-up risk lives — watch whether the Mg-doped variant retains the 0.025 S cm-1 transport.
insights.quote: Fig. 5: Electrochemical performance of the 4% Mg-doped (NBT)4/(BO)1 film as an electrolyte.

insights.claim: The work is led out of the University of Science and Technology Beijing and Hainan University with funding from the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the Beijing Outstanding Young Scientist Program and the Xiaomi Foundation's Xiaomi Young Talents Program.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
entities: University of Science and Technology Beijing
National Natural Science Foundation of China
insights.so_what: Chinese state plus corporate-foundation money (Xiaomi) is now underwriting frontier electrolyte materials — a marker of where next-generation fuel cell IP will be domiciled.
insights.quote: the Xiaomi Young Talents Program of the Xiaomi Foundation

insights.claim: The manuscript was received on 30 January 2024 and accepted 10 April 2026, a review cycle of more than two years for a headline energy-materials result.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A 26-month review lag means the underlying lab work is already old; assume competing groups have had time to replicate or leapfrog before treating this as novel.
